nameStory: The name "acephalus" comes from Greek meaning "without a head," which seems puzzling for any living creature! This likely refers to the weevil's distinctive snout (called a rostrum) being so prominent that it makes the actual head appear tiny or absent when viewed from certain angles. It's a classic example of how scientific names can capture a creature's most striking feature.
description: This tiny seed weevil is a member of the massive weevil family, easily recognized by their characteristic long snouts. Like all weevils, it has a hard, beetle-like body with the distinctive elongated rostrum extending from its head. These are truly minute insects, small enough that you'd need to look closely to spot them on their host plants. They're part of the incredibly diverse world of seed weevils that specialize in feeding on specific plants.

idTips.label: Elongated snout
idTips.description: Look for the classic weevil feature - a long, slender rostrum projecting forward from the head that looks almost like a tiny elephant trunk

idTips.label: Minute size
idTips.description: Extremely small - you'll need to peer closely at evening primrose leaves to spot these tiny beetles, often smaller than your fingernail

idTips.label: Hard wing covers
idTips.description: The wing covers (elytra) feel rigid and shell-like when gently touched, typical of beetles, with a slightly textured surface

idTips.label: Found on evening primrose
idTips.description: Almost always discovered feeding on the leaves of evening primrose plants, where they create small holes or notches in the foliage

idTips.label: Slow movement
idTips.description: Moves deliberately and slowly across leaf surfaces, often freezing in place when disturbed rather than flying away quickly

habitat: Look for these weevils in areas where evening primrose grows - typically disturbed soils, roadsides, old fields, and sunny openings in New England. They're closely tied to their host plant, so anywhere you find evening primrose blooming, you might discover these tiny specialists. They prefer the sunny, well-drained locations that evening primroses favor.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin emerging and becoming active on young evening primrose shoots as temperatures warm and new growth appears.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible feeding on evening primrose leaves, creating characteristic feeding damage on the foliage.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall while evening primrose plants remain green, though numbers may decline as plants begin to senesce.
seasonality.winter: Adults likely overwinter in leaf litter or soil debris near their host plants, remaining hidden and inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This weevil is so specialized that it has co-evolved with evening primrose plants over millions of years - it's essentially a living time capsule of plant-insect evolution, with its entire life strategy revolving around a single plant species that many people consider just a roadside weed!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny weevils on different plants, but the combination of evening primrose as host plant and the minute size makes identification clearer. Remember: right plant, tiny snout, slow movement - that's your evening primrose weevil.
contextualKnowledge: The term "seed weevil" can be confusing since this species actually feeds on leaves rather than seeds, unlike some of its relatives. The name refers more to the broader group's feeding habits rather than this specific species' behavior.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Acanthoscelidius species in our region, compare it with other minute weevils in the same family. Most other small weevils will be found on different host plants - if you're seeing tiny weevils specifically on evening primrose, you've likely found this species. Other weevils might be larger, have different snout proportions, or show different movement patterns.
